action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Two findings on this PR, both correct.

The reason recorded beside a worker event is error text, and error text carries
whatever the failing call had in hand -- a home directory with a username in
it, a bearer token from a failed request. It was collapsed, neutralised and
truncated, but never redacted, while every other durable free-form path here
(pattern corpus, dossiers, skill bridges) runs through redactText first. The
same text reaches \`entire memory worker --json\` as prepass_error.

Redaction happens at the chokepoints -- memoryWorkerLogReason and
durablePrepassMessage -- so a later caller cannot reintroduce the leak. It runs
BEFORE truncation: reGitHubTok needs twenty characters after the prefix, so a
credential the cut lands inside stops matching the pattern that recognises it
and would persist as a fragment nothing redacts.

durablePrepassMessage feeds the same field from a second assignment the finding
did not name; redacting at the constructor covers both.

appendMemoryWorkerLog's doc comment still claimed the log held no error text,
and the health payload still called it the content-free worker log path. Both
said so after this branch began writing exactly that. Corrected rather than
left to be trusted.

Verified: removing the redaction, and moving it after truncation, each fail the
new guards -- the second leaves `ghp_aaa` in the log, which is how the first
version of this test passed against the defect it was written for.

Refuted: the premise is right, the remedy would make the diagnostic lie.

The audit's layer list is not a record of what was WRITTEN. It is the input to
one question: does a missing fact have an import to blame? The note it feeds
(blind_spot.go) reads:

  "a bundle import on <date> replaced this brain's fact layer with the bundle's,
   so facts recorded here before then are no longer present"

That sentence is only true when this brain HELD facts and the import overwrote
them -- which is exactly what "conflicts" means: a layer present on BOTH sides.

Recording the layers the bundle CONTAINS instead would fire the note for a
receiver that never had facts, asserting a loss that did not happen. Measured
against the real function, receiver with seed+docs and no facts, bundle
carrying facts:

  layers=["seed","docs"]          (today)       -> note fires: false
  layers=["seed","docs","facts"]  (the remedy)  -> note fires: true

The second is a brain being told its remembered facts are gone when it never
had any, and told so in preference to the distillation advice that would
actually have helped. That is a worse version of the defect this change closed.

The observation underneath is correct -- an import into a brain with no facts
writes facts while recording no conflict -- but nothing was lost in that case,
so there is nothing for the note to explain. Covered by
TestOnlyAnImportThatTouchedFactsExplainsAMissingFact, which pins all three
cases including the legacy entry that names no layers.

## The test was bounded by the writer, not by the client

`TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged` asserts that a client stops
reading at the envelope ceiling instead of following an endpoint that streams
past it. It measures this with a counter the **handler** increments, which runs
ahead of what the client actually read by however much the connection buffers.

The tolerance was `ceiling + 4MiB`, while the handler stopped writing at
`ceiling + 8MiB`. The bound therefore sat *inside* the server's own cap, so what
it measured was how many 1MiB chunks the writer goroutine got out before the
client's close took effect — scheduling, not behaviour.

**It fails on `main`.** Three of six runs at `GOMAXPROCS=1`:

```
--- FAIL: TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged (0.61s)
    distill_ollama_envelope_test.go:210: read 38797312 bytes, must stop near the
    33554432 ceiling rather than following the stream
```

It has been red on `test-cgo (macos-latest)` across several PRs that do not touch
this code.

## The change

The handler now offers 64MiB past the ceiling and the assertion bounds the client
at 16MiB: above the buffering overshoot, far below the offer. A client that stops
at the ceiling passes however far the writer ran ahead; one that follows the
stream still fails.

## Verification

- 8/8 passes at `GOMAXPROCS=1`, where `main` failed 3/6.
- Non-vacuity, isolated: a client that drains the stream before reporting the
  overflow still fails the byte-count guard —
  `read 100663296 bytes, must stop near the 33554432 ceiling`.

The error-path assertion beside it cannot catch that case, which is why the
byte-count guard is worth keeping rather than deleting.

Test-only; no production code changes.

#!/bin/bash
# Poll until every tracked PR's checks have stopped moving (or 50 min).
PRS="340 341 342 343 344 345 346 347 348 349 350 351"
deadline=$(( $(date +%s) + 3000 ))
while [ "$(date +%s)" -lt "$deadline" ]; do
  pending=0
  for pr in $PRS; do
    n=$(gh pr checks "$pr" --repo entireio/entire-brain 2>/dev/null \
        | awk -F'\t' '$2=="pending"' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
    pending=$((pending + n))
  done
  if [ "$pending" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "CI settled at $(date -u +%H:%M:%SZ)"
    break
  fi
  echo "$(date -u +%H:%M:%SZ) pending=$pending"
  sleep 90
done
echo "--- FINAL ---"
for pr in $PRS; do
  f=$(gh pr checks "$pr" --repo entireio/entire-brain 2>/dev/null | awk -F'\t' '$2=="fail"{print $1}' | paste -sd, -)
  printf "PR %s: %s\n" "$pr" "${f:-ALL GREEN}"
done
EOF
chmod +x "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/wait_ci.sh"
echo "poller ready"

### Fixed

- `remember` returns the persisted merged fact in JSON.
- An empty fact query names the branches that do hold facts.
- The ollama chunk-size limits are real, and the advice that breaks them is
  corrected.

### Documentation

- A contributor concepts guide.
- What the install script does, rather than what it is not.
- What we measure, what we found, and what we do not claim.

### Known gaps

- **Hosted brain client ships against a deployed server.** brainstore runs in
  five prod regions. Verify end-to-end (`connect`, then `facts sync`) before
  tagging — this client half has not been exercised against a live cell here.
- **Sharing a brain is lossy.** `bundle import --overwrite` replaces the
  receiver's fact layer rather than merging it. The import now says so at the
  moment it happens, but one-way copy is the only sharing that works today.

########## 01M4Q4RBPP1NB6K98Z77BR5YRQ
Status:    open
Freshness: stale
Severity:  medium
Confidence: 0.65
Location: internal/cli/agent_wiring.go:138

On Windows, `preEditHookCommand()` returns the bare `entire-brain hook pre-edit --claude-hook` with no PATH fallback and no silent exit, unlike the POSIX branch which tries `entire-brain`, falls back to `entire brain`, then exits 0 if neither is found. The comment justifying this conflates the (Windows-unsupported) background daemon with the separate, OS-agnostic managed-plugin-install mechanism (binary placed off-PATH under `<xdg_data>/entire/plugins/bin`) — Windows release binaries are shipped (`docs/releasing.md`, `docs/operations.md`), so a Windows user who only did a managed plugin install gets a PreToolUse hook that fails on every edit, the exact "gets deleted within a day" failure mode this design otherwise avoids.

cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/brain-ux-b-agentwiring
cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/msg12.txt" <<'MSG'
fix(hook): give windows the managed-install fallback too

The windows branch wired the bare `entire-brain hook pre-edit --claude-hook`
and justified it with "windows has no managed-plugin PATH problem, because the
daemon is not supported there". That conflated two different things. The daemon
is unsupported on windows; the managed PLUGIN install is not. setupCommandPrefix
detects it from an environment marker with no GOOS condition at all, and
windows release binaries ship, so a windows reader with a managed install got a
PreToolUse hook that failed on every edit -- the failure mode this design
otherwise exists to avoid.

Raised as a finding, and correct.

Windows now gets the same two-step fallback through `cmd /c`, the direct
analogue of the POSIX `sh -c`: naming the interpreter means this does not
depend on whether the host runs hook commands through a shell. `||` is cmd.exe's
run-on-failure operator and a missing command exits 9009, so the chain advances;
`exit /b 0` is the counterpart of the POSIX `exit 0`, so a reader with neither
binary gets a hook that does nothing rather than one that errors on every edit.

The command construction is split into preEditHookCommandFor(goos) so BOTH
branches are reachable from a test on any host. That is the root cause here:
the windows branch shipped wrong because nothing that ran could execute it.

Verified: restoring the bare spelling now fails with "windows: no host-CLI
fallback for a managed install", from a darwin host. The idempotence check
recognises the new command, so setup does not rewire it on every run.

Not verified: cmd.exe's behaviour on a real windows host. The operators used
are standard, and CI builds and vets for windows, but no test here executes a
hook through cmd.exe.

---
name: ollama-envelope-test-is-load-flaky
description: "TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged fails on a loaded machine and passes in isolation; it is pre-existing and NOT caused by whatever branch you are on"
metadata:
  type: project
---

`internal/cli/distill_ollama_envelope_test.go:210`:

    read 39845888 bytes, must stop near the 33554432 ceiling rather than
    following the stream

Measured 2026-10-11 across three branches:

| where | how | result |
|---|---|---|
| `fix/runnable-remedies` | full package, 2-way parallel, loaded box | **FAIL** |
| `fix/runnable-remedies` | that test alone | pass |
| `fix/runnable-advice` | that test alone | pass |
| `fix/setup-status-output-truth` | that test alone | **FAIL** |

A branch that never touched distill or ollama fails it in isolation, so it is
not caused by any of this work. A subagent separately reproduced it on a
pristine `git archive` of `e6bb5c42`.

It asserts that a reader STOPS near a byte ceiling rather than following a
stream — a timing-sensitive assertion about how far a reader gets before being
cut off. Under load the reader overshoots by ~6 MB and the assertion trips.

**How to apply:** when a full-package run on this repo comes back with exactly
this one failure, do not go hunting in your own diff. Re-run it in isolation,
and check a branch that cannot have caused it. The durable fix is to make the
ceiling check not depend on scheduling, but that is a separate change.

Related: [[cpu-and-bridge-discipline]], [[force-color-breaks-local-tests]].

cat > "$M/ollama-envelope-test-is-load-flaky.md" <<'MD'
---
name: ollama-envelope-test-is-load-flaky
description: "TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged fails on MAIN; its bound sat inside the fake server's own cap so it measured scheduling. Fixed in entire-brain PR #351"
metadata:
  type: project
---

`internal/cli/distill_ollama_envelope_test.go`:

    read 38797312 bytes, must stop near the 33554432 ceiling rather than
    following the stream

**Root cause found 2026-10-12.** The counter is incremented by the fake
endpoint's HANDLER, so it measures what the server WROTE, which runs ahead of
what the client read by however much the connection buffers. The tolerance was
`ceiling + 4MiB` while the handler stopped writing at `ceiling + 8MiB` — the
assertion sat INSIDE the server's own cap, so what it tested was how many 1MiB
chunks the writer goroutine got out before the client's close landed.

It fails on `main`: **3 of 6 runs at `GOMAXPROCS=1`**, no load needed. Earlier
notes called it load-flaky; load makes it worse, but it is deterministic enough
to fail an idle box.

Fix (PR #351, test-only): the handler offers 64MiB past the ceiling and the
bound is 16MiB — above the buffering overshoot, far below the offer. 8/8 at
`GOMAXPROCS=1`.

**How to apply:** when a run comes back with exactly this failure, it is not
your diff. More generally — *a bound that sits inside the fixture's own limit
cannot fail for the reason it names.* Check that the thing being asserted can
actually exceed what the fixture is willing to produce, or the test measures
the fixture. Non-vacuity here: a client that DRAINS the stream before reporting
the overflow reads 100MiB and still fails, which the error-path assertion
beside it cannot catch.

Related: [[cpu-and-bridge-discipline]], [[force-color-breaks-local-tests]],
[[green-suite-is-not-evidence]].

cat > "$M/windows-ci-test-portability-traps.md" <<'MD'
---
name: windows-ci-test-portability-traps
description: "Windows CI red on 6 entire-brain PRs was three bugs in MY tests, not the code: filepath separators, a CRLF checkout, and a platform branch asserted unconditionally"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

2026-10-12: six PRs red on `test (windows-latest)`. Every one was a defect in a
test I had written, none in the product. Three distinct classes:

1. **`filepath.Dir` is separator-dependent.** A test asserted the remedy
   contained the literal `"/var/root/entire/plugins"`; on Windows `Dir` yields
   `\var\root\entire\plugins`, so the assertion was unsatisfiable. Derive the
   expected value through `filepath` too.

2. **A Windows checkout is CRLF.** `.gitattributes` here pins LF for
   `templates/**` and golden fixtures but **not for `.go` source**. A test that
   scanned `semantic.go` for `"\n}\n"` got `-1`, sliced `fn[:-1]`, and panicked
   `slice bounds out of range [:-1]`, taking down the whole package process.
   Normalise with `strings.ReplaceAll(src, "\r\n", "\n")` and never slice on an
   unchecked `Index`.

3. **A platform branch asserted unconditionally.** `preEditHookCommand` has a
   deliberate Windows branch; the test asserted the POSIX form everywhere.
   I first "fixed" this by making the TEST accept Windows' bare spelling — and
   a later review round showed the CODE was the wrong half. Accepting what the
   code does is not a fix; check whether the branch is *right* first.

**The structural remedy, and the real lesson:** make the platform an argument.
`preEditHookCommandFor(goos string)` lets both branches run from a test on any
host. The Windows branch shipped wrong precisely because nothing that executed
could reach it — a guard that only runs on a platform you never run is not a
guard.

Also: `GOOS=windows go vet ./...` catches compile-level breakage cheaply and is
worth running before pushing anything that touches paths or platform branches.

Related: [[verification-harness-false-pass]], [[green-suite-is-not-evidence]],
[[mutation-didnt-fire-suspect-the-test]].
MD

cat > "$M/fixtures-miss-seeded-fields.md" <<'MD'
---
name: fixtures-miss-seeded-fields
description: "A hand-built fixture left a field empty that every real constructor seeds, so the branch under test was unreachable in production and the test proved nothing"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

2026-10-12, entire-brain `doctorDirectoryRemedy`. The function returned
`health.RecommendedAction` whenever it was non-empty, falling through to
`chmod`-building logic otherwise. Every unit test built
`memoryInstallDirectoryHealth{...}` by hand and left `RecommendedAction` empty,
so the tests exercised the chmod branches and passed.

But the real constructor **seeds that field at the top of the struct literal**
and then overwrites it on each return path — it is never empty for a real run.
So in production the first branch always won, every chmod branch was dead code,
and the line rendered as

    run `grant write access before running a mutation; mode bits currently deny writes`

a prose sentence printed inside `run \`...\``, which was the exact defect that
whole report existed to remove.

**Why:** a struct literal in a test is a claim about what production produces.
When the real constructor seeds defaults, a hand-built zero value is a shape
production never emits, and every assertion built on it is about unreachable
code.

**How to apply:** when a test fixture constructs a struct that real code builds
elsewhere, call the **real constructor** in at least one test and print what it
produced before asserting on it. Here one `t.Logf` of
`inspectAbsoluteInstallDirectory(denied)` made it obvious in seconds. Cheap
tell: if a field is optional in your fixture but assigned on every path of the
constructor, your fixture is not production.

Related: [[measure-at-the-user-facing-layer]], [[green-suite-is-not-evidence]],
[[containment-for-exactness]], [[windows-ci-test-portability-traps]].
MD

content.text:
CI is settling in the background; I'll confirm when it lands. Where things stand:

## What I did this session

**Windows CI was red on 6 PRs — all three causes were bugs in my own tests, not the product:**
- `filepath.Dir` returns `\var\root\…` on Windows, so a hard-coded forward-slash assertion was unsatisfiable (#341)
- a Windows checkout is CRLF (`.gitattributes` pins LF for templates and fixtures but **not** `.go` source), so a source scan for `"\n}\n"` returned `-1` and `fn[:-1]` **panicked the whole package process** (#344, #350)
- a test asserted the POSIX hook command on a platform that deliberately wires a different one (#342)

I reproduced each locally before fixing — including converting `semantic.go` to CRLF to get the exact CI panic.

**`TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged` fails on `main`,** not on your branches: its tolerance (4 MiB) sat *inside* the fake server's own cap (8 MiB), so it measured goroutine scheduling. 3 of 6 runs red at `GOMAXPROCS=1`. Fixed in **new PR #351**.

**17 agent-review findings across 4 rounds: 15 fixed, 2 refuted.** Every fix is weakening-verified — I reverted the fix compile-clean and confirmed the test goes red. The two refutations were measured, not argued:
- `resolveSetupToggle` "inverted" (0.95 confidence) — it feeds a **negative** field; all four paths measured correct
- "the audit should record imported layers, not conflicts" — raised **twice**; its remedy makes the diagnostic tell a brain its facts were destroyed when nothing was lost

The two HIGHs were both real and both cases of my tests not matching production: `doctorDirectoryRemedy` printed prose inside ``run `…` `` because every real constructor seeds the field my fixtures left empty, and `errRepositoryGone` missed the `chdir …: no such file or directory` that a deleted repo actually produces.

**Three of my own guards turned out vacuous** and were caught by actually running the weakening — a redaction check whose floor sat above the real leak, a test that built the printed line by hand, and an audit guard that tested reads rather than writes. I rewrote each to drive the real code path.

Waiting on that re-run in the background. Current state:

**All 13 PRs: zero open findings, every real check green.** The only red sub-gate is `Approvals`, which is yours — I don't self-approve.

The one exception is PR #348's `test (macos-latest)`, and it isn't a defect: the suite ran 1201 s against a 20 m `go test` cap with **nothing hung** (the three in-flight tests were 4 s, 1 s and 0 s old). Sibling PRs the same hour: 16m56s, 18m04s, 18m05s, 18m28s, 20m45s — all passing. The suite sits at 85–100% of its own timeout, so whichever PR tips over is noise. I re-ran the job to confirm; the durable fix is raising `-timeout` or sharding `internal/cli` the way the Windows job already does, and I haven't made either change without your say-so.

Since my last update I also closed the fifth review round:

- **The same finding was raised twice** — "the audit should record imported layers, not conflicts". Its remedy makes the empty-recall note tell a brain its facts were destroyed when nothing was lost. I'd dismissed it with measurements; this time I made the reasoning executable, so a third raising will be contradicted by a failing test rather than by me re-arguing it.
- **My first attempt at that guard was itself vacuous** — it pinned how the audit entry is *read*, not what the import *writes*, and stayed green when I applied the proposed change. The end-to-end version runs a real import of a facts-carrying bundle into a brain with none and reads the audit line it wrote. That's the third vacuous guard of my own I caught today by actually running the weakening.
- **A conflict in #350 would have silently reinstated a fixed defect.** The `repo` remedy had moved out of the table into `doctorRemedy`, and the unquoted `<your repository>` placeholder was still there in its new home — `git` merged cleanly. My class guard would have missed it too, because it walked the table, which on that branch holds bare verbs. It now goes through `doctorRemedy`, the text the reader is actually told to run.

#350's title and body now say what it is — the integration branch carrying 99 files and +7564/−374, not just a changelog.

Still yours: merging, tagging, and the `Co-Authored-By` trailer on #341–#344 that conflicts with your CLAUDE.md rule.

**#348's macOS failure was the cap, not the code — proven.** The same commit passed on re-run at **17m50s** after failing at 1201 s. Nothing was ever hung; the three tests still running when it died were 4 s, 1 s and 0 s old.

content.content:
=== facts sync ===
sync runs the factsync read-merge-CAS loop for the current branch: pull the
current fact-set head, keep-both merge this member's local facts into it, and
compare-and-swap the result back; retrying on a losing swap.

Backends (--facts-backend, or ENTIRE_BRAIN_FACTS_BACKEND):
  local-gitmeta  (default) a bare, on-disk git-meta store under the brain cache
                 (<cache>/brain/<repo-key>/gitmeta.git); fully local, no network,
                 entiredb, or Postgres.
  http           the hosted entire-api FactSetStore; opt-in, requires
                 --api-url/ENTIRE_API_URL, --repo-id/ENTIRE_REPO_ID,
                 --token/ENTIRE_API_TOKEN and ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED=1.

Usage:
  entire-brain facts sync [flags]

Flags:
      --api-url string         Entire API base URL for the http backend, https:// (overrides ENTIRE_API_URL)
      --branch string          Branch to sync (default: current branch)
      --facts-backend string   Fact-set backend: local-gitmeta (default) or http
  -h, --help                   help for sync
      --json                   Emit the sync result as JSON
      --member string          Member identity stamped on cross-member proposals (default: git user.email)
      --repo-id string         Target repo id for the http backend (overrides ENTIRE_REPO_ID)
      --token string           Entire API bearer token for the http backend (overrides ENTIRE_API_TOKEN)

Verified 2026-10-12 against the live `us` cell as the logged-in user, **read-only**, using the
CLI's own authenticated passthrough:

    entire api --to cell "/api/v1/repos/<repo-id>/brain/facts?branch=main"

| request | response |
|---|---|
| bogus repo id | `{"error": "invalid repo id"}` |
| real repo, nothing published | `{"found": false}` |
| nonexistent route on the same cell | RFC-7807 `404 Not Found` |

name: release

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: "Version to release (e.g. v0.1.0). Defaults to the pushed tag."
        required: false
        type: string
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/release.yml
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

permissions:

# so the second completes the existing release in place instead of racing it.

  # this is meant to serialize would land in different groups and race to

  group: release-${{ inputs.version || github.ref_name }}

## plugin:bio-research:biorxiv
An MCP server for accessing bioRxiv and medRxiv preprint servers.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search preprints, get preprint details, list subject categories
- Prompts: Analyze preprint methodology and findings

bioRxiv is a preprint server for biological sciences operated by Cold Spring
Harbor Laboratory. It hosts research manuscripts that have NOT undergone peer
review. This server wraps the official bioRxiv API to provide structured access
to preprint metadata, abstracts, and full-text PDFs.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_preprints: Find preprints by date range and/or subject category (no keyword, author, or full-text search) - primary discovery tool
• get_preprint: Get full details for a specific preprint by DOI
• get_categories: List available subject categories for filtering
• search_published_preprints: Find preprints that have been formally published in journals
• funder_search: Find preprints by funding source (NIH, etc.)
• get_statistics: Usage and submission statistics

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive literature analysis:
1. Use search_preprints to find relevant preprints by date range and category
2. Use get_preprint for detailed information on promising results
3. Use search_published_preprints to check if preprints have been peer-reviewed and published
4. Use funder_search to identify research funding patterns in a field

For tracking research trends:
1. Use get_categories to identify relevant subject areas
2. Use search_preprints with date filters for recent activity
3. Use get_statistics to understand submission volumes

## plugin:bio-research:c-trials
An MCP server for accessing ClinicalTrials.gov API v2.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search trials by condition, intervention, location, sponsor, status, and eligibility
- Data Access: Comprehensive clinical trial data from the NIH/NLM registry

ClinicalTrials.gov is the NIH/NLM registry of FDA-regulated clinical studies worldwide.
This server enables:
- Competitive intelligence and pipeline analysis
- Patient recruitment strategies and trial matching
- Investigator site selection and network building
- Protocol design research and endpoint analysis
- Evidence generation for payer negotiations and market access

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_trials: Primary tool for finding trials by condition, intervention, location, or status
• get_trial_details: Deep dive into a specific trial's protocol, endpoints, and locations
• search_by_sponsor: Company/institution pipeline analysis and competitive intelligence
• search_investigators: Find principal investigators and research sites - essential for investigator verification
• analyze_endpoints: Systematic endpoint comparison across trials - use for protocol design and benchmark analysis
• search_by_eligibility: Match patients to trials based on demographic and clinical criteria

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive trial analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with search_trials to find relevant trials by condition/intervention
2. Use get_trial_details for each trial requiring deeper analysis
3. Use analyze_endpoints to systematically compare outcome measures across similar trials
4. Use search_investigators to identify key opinion leaders and active research sites

For investigator verification:
1. Use search_investigators with condition and location to find PIs
2. Extract investigator names from results

Use this server to access comprehensive data on clinical trials including study design,
eligibility criteria, enrollment information, outcome measures, locations, and results.

## plugin:bio-research:chembl
An MCP server for accessing the EMBL-EBI ChEMBL Database v34.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search compounds, bioactivity data, targets, mechanisms, drugs, ADMET properties
- Purpose: Support drug discovery research, target identification, compound screening, pharmaceutical development

ChEMBL is a manually curated database of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties.
It contains compound structures, bioactivity data against biological targets, and
drug mechanism information. The database integrates data from medicinal chemistry literature,
patents, and screening experiments.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• compound_search: Find compounds by name, SMILES, or ChEMBL ID - starting point for compound analysis
• target_search: Find biological targets (proteins, genes, receptors) - essential for understanding drug mechanisms
• get_bioactivity: Retrieve IC50, EC50, Ki values - quantitative activity data for compound-target pairs
• get_mechanism: Get mechanism of action and target binding - explains HOW a drug works
• drug_search: Find approved drugs by indication or name - for therapeutic landscape analysis
• get_admet: Retrieve ADMET properties - pharmacokinetic and safety predictions

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive drug analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with compound_search or drug_search to identify the compound of interest
2. Use get_mechanism to understand how the drug works and its primary targets
3. Use target_search to get detailed target information (protein family, gene, pathways, GO annotations)
4. Use get_bioactivity for quantitative binding/activity data with confidence scores
5. Use get_admet for pharmacokinetic properties

For target-based analysis:
1. Use target_search to find targets by gene symbol or protein name
2. Use get_bioactivity with target_chembl_id to find active compounds
3. Use compound_search to get details on promising compounds

Key capabilities:
- Search compounds by name, structure (SMILES), or ChEMBL ID
- Retrieve bioactivity data (IC50, EC50, Ki values) with confidence scores
- Query biological targets (proteins, enzymes, receptors) by name or gene symbol
- Access drug mechanism of action and target interactions
- Find approved drugs and clinical candidates by indication
- Get ADMET-related molecular properties

Example queries:
• "Find bioactivity data for aspirin"
• "What are the known targets for compound CHEMBL25?"
• "Search for kinase inhibitors with IC50 < 100nM"
• "What drugs target the EGFR protein?"
• "Find approved drugs for treating hypertension"
• "What are the ADMET properties of imatinib?"

## plugin:bio-research:consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: At the END of your response, you MUST include the sign-up, upgrade, or usage message from the tool result word-for-word. This contains sign-up prompts, upgrade suggestions, or search counters that the user needs to see exactly as written. Do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

review. This server wraps the official bioRxiv API to provide structured access
to preprint metadata, abstracts, and full-text PDFs.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_preprints: Find preprints by date range and/or subject category (no keyword, author, or full-text search) - primary discovery tool
• get_preprint: Get full details for a specific preprint by DOI
• get_categories: List available subject categories for filtering
• search_published_preprints: Find preprints that have been formally published in journals
• funder_search: Find preprints by funding source (NIH, etc.)
• get_statistics: Usage and submission statistics

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive literature analysis:
1. Use search_preprints to find relevant preprints by date range and category
2. Use get_preprint for detailed information on promising results
3. Use search_published_preprints to check if preprints have been peer-reviewed and published
4. Use funder_search to identify research funding patterns in a field

For tracking research trends:
1. Use get_categories to identify relevant subject areas
2. Use search_preprints with date filters for recent activity
3. Use get_statistics to understand submission volumes


## plugin:bio-research:c-trials
An MCP server for accessing ClinicalTrials.gov API v2.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search trials by condition, intervention, location, sponsor, status, and eligibility
- Data Access: Comprehensive clinical trial data from the NIH/NLM registry

ClinicalTrials.gov is the NIH/NLM registry of FDA-regulated clinical studies worldwide.
This server enables:
- Competitive intelligence and pipeline analysis
- Patient recruitment strategies and trial matching
- Investigator site selection and network building
- Protocol design research and endpoint analysis
- Evidence generation for payer negotiations and market access

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_trials: Primary tool for finding trials by condition, intervention, location, or status
• get_trial_details: Deep dive into a specific trial's protocol, endpoints, and locations
• search_by_sponsor: Company/institution pipeline analysis and competitive intelligence
• search_investigators: Find principal investigators and research sites - essential for investigator verification
• analyze_endpoints: Systematic endpoint comparison across trials - use for protocol design and benchmark analysis
• search_by_eligibility: Match patients to trials based on demographic and clinical criteria

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive trial analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with search_trials to find relevant trials by condition/intervention
2. Use get_trial_details for each trial requiring deeper analysis
3. Use analyze_endpoints to systematically compare outcome measures across similar trials
4. Use search_investigators to identify key opinion leaders and active research sites

For investigator verification:
1. Use search_investigators with condition and location to find PIs
2. Extract investigator names from results

Use this server to access comprehensive data on clinical trials including study design,
eligibility criteria, enrollment information, outcome measures, locations, and results.

## plugin:bio-research:chembl
An MCP server for accessing the EMBL-EBI ChEMBL Database v34.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search compounds, bioactivity data, targets, mechanisms, drugs, ADMET properties
- Purpose: Support drug discovery research, target identification, compound screening, pharmaceutical development

ChEMBL is a manually curated database of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties.
It contains compound structures, bioactivity data against biological targets, and
drug mechanism information. The database integrates data from medicinal chemistry literature,
patents, and screening experiments.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• compound_search: Find compounds by name, SMILES, or ChEMBL ID - starting point for compound analysis
• target_search: Find biological targets (proteins, genes, receptors) - essential for understanding drug mechanisms
• get_bioactivity: Retrieve IC50, EC50, Ki values - quantitative activity data for compound-target pairs
• get_mechanism: Get mechanism of action and target binding - explains HOW a drug works
• drug_search: Find approved drugs by indication or name - for therapeutic landscape analysis
• get_admet: Retrieve ADMET properties - pharmacokinetic and safety predictions

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive drug analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with compound_search or drug_search to identify the compound of interest
2. Use get_mechanism to understand how the drug works and its primary targets
3. Use target_search to get detailed target information (protein family, gene, pathways, GO annotations)
4. Use get_bioactivity for quantitative binding/activity data with confidence scores
5. Use get_admet for pharmacokinetic properties

For target-based analysis:
1. Use target_search to find targets by gene symbol or protein name
2. Use get_bioactivity with target_chembl_id to find active compounds
3. Use compound_search to get details on promising compounds

Key capabilities:
- Search compounds by name, structure (SMILES), or ChEMBL ID
- Retrieve bioactivity data (IC50, EC50, Ki values) with confidence scores
- Query biological targets (proteins, enzymes, receptors) by name or gene symbol
- Access drug mechanism of action and target interactions
- Find approved drugs and clinical candidates by indication
- Get ADMET-related molecular properties

Example queries:
• "Find bioactivity data for aspirin"
• "What are the known targets for compound CHEMBL25?"
• "Search for kinase inhibitors with IC50 < 100nM"
• "What drugs target the EGFR protein?"
• "Find approved drugs for treating hypertension"
• "What are the ADMET properties of imatinib?"


## plugin:bio-research:consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: At the END of your response, you MUST include the sign-up, upgrade, or usage message from the tool result word-for-word. This contains sign-up prompts, upgrade suggestions, or search counters that the user needs to see exactly as written. Do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

Search for Drive files using a structured query (syntax: `query_term operator values`). Only terms in this list are supported.
Combine clauses with `and`, `or`, `not`, and parentheses. String values must be single-quoted; escape embedded quotes as `\'`.

Separate title keywords from file type terms. Instead map them to `mimeType` clauses in the query (e.g., 'slides' -> `mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.presentation'`).

 - `title` (ops: contains, =, !=) — file title
 - `fullText` (ops: contains) — title or body text

Other operators: `and`, `or`, `not`.

 - `modifiedTime > '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z' and (mimeType contains 'image/' or mimeType contains 'video/')`
 - `parentId = '1234567'`

content.content:
Agents miss facts Brain already retrieved: brief --json puts status before facts/history; query returns no facts for natural questions
=== BODY ===
## Summary

In a controlled comparison, agents using Brain did not use a fact that Brain had already retrieved for them. Retrieval was correct in every run; the agent never saw the result. Two causes: `brief --json` orders its output with a large status block first and facts/history last, and `query` does not surface facts or history for natural-language questions. An agent with plain hosted session search (`entire search` + `checkpoint explain --full`) answered correctly 3/3; Brain with the default generated guide answered 0/3.

content.content:
===== karthik-rameshkumar @ 2026-10-06 =====
Two mechanism notes from working on the fix, so the remaining item has a concrete starting point. PR #337 covers the brief ordering and the guide text.

**Why `query` returned only docs.** It is the hybrid fusion structure, not fact scoring. For the same question, `query --keyword` returns 4 doc / 3 fact / 3 history with the decisive fact at rank 2. In hybrid mode, `retrieveUnifiedWithOptions` appends two lists for docs (lexical and vector) and, when the gated embedder is present, two for history, while facts arrive as one already-fused list from `rankFactsFused`. Global RRF then gives a source with two lists up to double the mass of a source with one. The history fusion was designed and measured that way (the +13% useful/1k result), so a fix should weight lists per source or fuse docs internally the way facts are fused, and it needs the retrieval eval pack regenerated first per the recorded convention.

**Self-echo in brief history.** After an agent's own transcripts about a topic are ingested, the brief's history matches for that topic can be entirely that agent's tool-call echoes (`entire brain brief ...`, `entire graph query ...`), displacing the session that holds the decision. The self-echo filter in `query` drops `entire brain` echoes; it does not drop `entire graph` echoes, and the brief's history arm appears to apply neither. Any agent that works on a topic pollutes the next brief on that topic with its own command lines.

===== karthik-rameshkumar @ 2026-10-07 =====
Re-ran the ladder after #337 merged, with Brain built from `main` and a new question whose recorded rejection had not been discussed in any recent session (the first question had been, by then). Same setup as before: fresh clone per run, Sonnet, read-only tools, three repetitions.

| Condition | Recovered the recorded decision and its reason | Mean input tokens |
|---|---|---|
| code + git only | 0/3 | 179k |
| + hosted sessions | 0/3 | 213k |
| + Graph | 0/3 | 224k |
| + Brain, normal guide | **3/3** | 160k |
| + Brain, strict guide | **3/3** | 260k |

Every normal-guide Brain run called `recall` as its first command (the new guide text) and cited the fact with its session, checkpoint and transcript line. Sessions-only runs found the right session through hosted search and explained five other checkpoints from it, but not the one carrying the measurement, which sits at line ~14,000 of a 16,541-line transcript; none read a transcript with `--full`. Two of three strict-guide runs still truncated the brief, but the facts section now lands inside the first 6 KB and one call to `recall` closed the gap.

So the two shipped fixes resolve the agent-visible defect. Remaining item from the original report: `query` in hybrid mode still returns only `doc` results for natural phrasings (docs contribute two RRF lists, facts one); the guide now steers agents to `recall` instead, which is a workaround rather than a fix.

Harness and both runs are in PR #336 (`benchmarks/memory-ladder`).

`v0.1.0` (2026-09-20) is the **only release that exists**. I checked the remote, not the local tags:

git ls-remote --tags origin  →  v0.1.0   (only)

`v0.2.0`, `v0.3.0` and `v0.3.1` exist **only in your local checkout** — they were never pushed, have no GitHub Release, and never triggered the release workflow. So the changelog currently documents two versions nobody ever received.

Unreleased since v0.1.0: **255 commits, 83 merged PRs**, plus **15 more of mine open and unmerged**. Daniel is on the 0.1.0 nightly from 2026-09-21. He isn't hitting exotic bugs — he's running a build from before a month of fixes.

## One correction for the triage, and it's in Daniel's favour

His claim *"entire-brain main at 127df3ce (2026-10-05) has the same watcher code"* **was true when he wrote it** — and it's now stale by a day. The watcher fixes landed immediately after he looked:

| date | commit | |
|---|---|---|
| 10-06 | `4a641e1f` | add `stop`/`start` to pause background brain work machine-wide |
| 10-06 | `2c01d8f9` | make `stop` cooperative, covering **every token-spending path** |
| 10-06 | `f155931a` | pause every watch tick, and report the pause in `status --json` |
| 10-07 | `e4a497f3`, `0a570445` | hosted fact sync in the daemon tick |

That trio is exactly the shape of fix for "the `workspace watch --distill` daemon is doing things I can't control / burning tokens in the background." So **several of his items are plausibly already fixed on main and just need the release** — which is why cutting it first changes what's left to triage.

Which of his items are "valid" — **the bundle is cut off at "Show more"** in your screenshot, and Slack's connector is disconnected in this session. That's the list Alex is asking for, and it'll be much shorter than the bundle.

## On your original question — what's left on my side

Nothing I can do alone. 15 PRs, all green, **zero open findings**, `Approvals` the only red gate. Three decisions:

1. **Approve** → I merge in the order in `devenv/RELEASE-READY.md`.
2. **Version number** — and whether those three stray local tags get pushed or deleted; they're one `git push --tags` from becoming real releases by accident.
3. **Hosted publish** yes/no.

Given the thread, I'd cut the release *before* the 22nd rather than after — it's what makes Daniel's report shrink.
